CAIRO, Egypt (CNN)  -- Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak met Thursday in Cairo amid escalating cross-border violence between Israel and Hamas. Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni meets Thursday with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo. The session follows the end of a tenuous 6-month-long cease-fire between the Israeli military and Hamas militants in Gaza. Egypt mediated the first truce and is trying to negotiate an extension despite what Israel says are dozens of rockets fired by Hamas into the Jewish state this week. Livni criticized Hamas after her meeting with Mubarak. "Hamas needs to understand that Israel's basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn't mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population," she said, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. "Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change." Egypt expressed concern about a deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza, an Israeli Foreign Ministry statement said. The Egyptian Foreign Ministry said this week that it would help countries and organizations deliver aid through Egyptian territory to Palestinians in Gaza. Livni also met with the head of Egyptian intelligence Thursday and is scheduled to talk with the Egyptian foreign minister. Israeli military officials said Hamas militants fired more than 65 rockets into southern Israel on Wednesday. Meanwhile, the Israeli air force said it killed a Hamas militant who was part of a group launching the rockets into Israel. An Israeli police spokesman said no one had been injured in the latest barrage of rocket attacks. But emergency workers with Magen David Adom, Israel's Red Cross agency, treated 57 people suffering from shock, half of them children, an agency official said, adding that 200 ambulances were standing by in the area. "I think the circumstances are extremely tragic, that Muslim zealots of Hamas have decided to shatter and ruin the Christmas celebrations of the Christian brothers in the Holy Land, both in the West Bank and of course in Gaza itself," Israeli Welfare Minister Isaac Herzog said. "If things deteriorate further, then of course we'll have to take necessary action, which will be very painful," Herzog said, adding that civilians had gathered in shelters in southern Israel to try to stay safe amid the rocket attacks. Asked about the possibility of Israel coming up with a new strategy, Herzog responded, "The new strategy could be, of course, an all-out conflict against Hamas, which is a possibility that voices in Israel are calling for. We are trying to show restraint." Hamas is a Palestinian Islamic fundamentalist organization whose military wing, Izzedine al Qassam, has admitted responsibility for terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians as well as attacks against the Israeli military. Israel and the U.S. State Department consider Hamas a terrorist organization, though it also operates an extensive social services network in the territories. Mark Regev, spokesman for Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, said, "Our position is clear: We will answer quiet with quiet, and we will answer attacks with measures designed to protect our people." Olmert has threatened to respond to the ongoing attacks. The truce between the Hamas government in Gaza and Israel expired Friday. Under the Egyptian-brokered deal, Hamas agreed to end militant attacks on Israel from Gaza, and Israel agreed to halt raids inside the territory and ease its blockade on humanitarian goods. In reality, the truce had started breaking down two months ago. Rocket attacks by militants became more frequent, and Israel resumed airstrikes inside Gaza. "We really appreciate the Egyptian efforts. ...," Herzog said. "The Egyptians have tried endlessly and tirelessly in the past few weeks to bring Hamas back to cease-fire mode." Olmert said Sunday that Israel will "take the necessary measures" to respond to the rocket attacks and "will know when to respond correctly and with the necessary responsibility." "A responsible government is neither eager for battle, nor does it shy away from it," he said.

“I think the circumstances are extremely tragic, that Muslim zealots of Hamas have decided to shatter and ruin the Christmas celebrations of the Christian brothers in the Holy Land, both in the West Bank and of course in Gaza itself,” Israeli Welfare Minister Isaac Herzog said.

Asked about the possibility of Israel adopting a new strategy, Herzog responded, “The new strategy could be, of course, an all-out conflict against Hamas, which is a possibility that voices in Israel are calling for. We are trying to show restraint.”

CAIRO, Egypt (CNN) — Israel’s foreign minister, Tzipi Livni, held talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo on Thursday as violence across the Israel-Gaza border intensified between Israel and Hamas.

The meeting came shortly after a fragile six-month cease-fire between Israel’s military and Hamas militants in Gaza came to an end. Egypt, which helped broker the original truce, has been seeking to arrange an extension, even as Israel says Hamas has fired dozens of rockets into Israeli territory this week.

After meeting with Mubarak, Livni sharply criticized Hamas.

“Hamas needs to understand that Israel’s basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn’t mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population,” she said, according to Israel’s Foreign Ministry. “Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change.”

A statement from the Israeli Foreign Ministry said Egypt voiced concern about worsening humanitarian conditions in Gaza. Earlier in the week, Egypt’s Foreign Ministry said it would assist countries and organizations in sending aid through Egyptian territory to Palestinians in Gaza.

Livni also met Thursday with Egypt’s intelligence chief and was expected to hold discussions with Egypt’s foreign minister.

Israeli military officials said Hamas militants launched more than 65 rockets into southern Israel on Wednesday. At the same time, Israel’s air force said it killed a Hamas militant who had been among a group firing rockets into Israel.

An Israeli police spokesman said the most recent wave of rocket fire caused no injuries. However, Magen David Adom, Israel’s Red Cross organization, said its emergency teams treated 57 people for shock, about half of them children. An official with the agency also said 200 ambulances were on standby in the area.

Israeli Welfare Minister Isaac Herzog described the situation as deeply troubling.

“I think the circumstances are extremely tragic, that Muslim zealots of Hamas have decided to shatter and ruin the Christmas celebrations of the Christian brothers in the Holy Land, both in the West Bank and of course in Gaza itself,” Herzog said.

He added that if the situation worsened, Israel would have to take “necessary action,” which he said would be “very painful.” Herzog also said civilians in southern Israel had taken refuge in shelters to protect themselves from the rocket attacks.

When asked whether Israel might adopt a new strategy, Herzog said, “The new strategy could be, of course, an all-out conflict against Hamas, which is a possibility that voices in Israel are calling for. We are trying to show restraint.”

Hamas is a Palestinian Islamic fundamentalist group. Its armed wing, Izzedine al Qassam, has claimed responsibility for terrorist attacks on Israeli civilians and for assaults on the Israeli military. Israel and the U.S. State Department classify Hamas as a terrorist organization, although the group also runs a broad social services network in the Palestinian territories.

Mark Regev, spokesman for Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, said Israel’s stance was straightforward.

“Our position is clear: We will answer quiet with quiet, and we will answer attacks with measures designed to protect our people,” Regev said.

Olmert has warned that Israel will respond to the continuing rocket fire.

The cease-fire between Israel and the Hamas-led government in Gaza expired Friday. Under the agreement mediated by Egypt, Hamas was to stop militant attacks from Gaza into Israel, while Israel was to end raids inside Gaza and loosen its restrictions on humanitarian supplies.

In practice, however, the truce had begun unraveling two months earlier. Militants increased rocket fire, and Israel restarted airstrikes in Gaza.

“We really appreciate the Egyptian efforts,” Herzog said. “The Egyptians have tried endlessly and tirelessly in the past few weeks to bring Hamas back to cease-fire mode.”

On Sunday, Olmert said Israel would “take the necessary measures” in response to the rocket attacks and would determine the proper time to act “correctly and with the necessary responsibility.”

“A responsible government is neither eager for battle, nor does it shy away from it,” he said.

*December 2008* — Tensions between Israel and Hamas escalated sharply in and around the Gaza Strip as Egyptian mediators sought to prevent the collapse of a fragile cease-fire and Israeli officials warned that continued rocket fire could prompt military action.

The truce, brokered by Egypt in June, had reduced cross-border violence for several months but came under growing strain in late 2008. Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups resumed rocket and mortar fire into southern Israel, targeting communities including Sderot and areas near Ashkelon. Israel said the attacks endangered civilians and made normal life impossible for residents near the Gaza border.

Hamas said the cease-fire had been undermined by Israeli military operations and the continued blockade of Gaza, which Israel tightened after Hamas took control of the territory in 2007. The group demanded that crossings into Gaza be opened more fully as part of any renewed calm.

Egypt, which has served as the main intermediary between Israel and Hamas, attempted to broker an extension of the cease-fire. Egyptian officials held contacts with Hamas representatives and other Palestinian factions while also relaying messages to Israel. Cairo urged both sides to avoid escalation, warning that a renewed conflict would worsen conditions in Gaza and destabilize the region.

Israeli leaders, however, signaled that patience was running out. Officials said the government was considering a range of responses if rocket fire continued, including a broader military operation against Hamas targets in Gaza. Israeli defense officials said the army was preparing for possible action while the government weighed diplomatic and security options.

Residents in southern Israel were told to remain alert as rocket sirens continued to sound. In Gaza, residents braced for possible Israeli strikes amid shortages of fuel, electricity, and basic supplies linked to the blockade and border restrictions.

The cease-fire formally expired in mid-December, leaving Egypt’s mediation efforts uncertain and raising fears that the cycle of rocket attacks and Israeli retaliation could develop into a wider confrontation.
